blocks.text: A carbon-fibre bicycle fork is cut from sheets in which every fibre runs along the fork leg. Along the leg the material has a higher stiffness per unit mass (specific stiffness) than steel, yet a hammer tap across the fibres of an offcut can split it. The two responses come from one simple idea: the fibres and the matrix share load in different ways depending on the direction of loading.

blocks.markdown: A unidirectional **fibre composite** consists of strong, stiff fibres (carbon, glass, aramid) in a compliant matrix (epoxy). The fibres carry most of the load, while the matrix holds them in place, transfers load between them and protects them. The volume fraction $V_f$ of fibre and $V_m=1-V_f$ of matrix are the main design variables; the simple *rules of mixtures* give the stiffness in two limiting directions.

blocks.title: Longitudinal and transverse directions
blocks.text: The **longitudinal** direction is parallel to the fibres, the **transverse** direction perpendicular to them. Longitudinal loading deforms fibres and matrix by the same strain (iso-strain, parallel springs); transverse loading passes the same stress through fibre and matrix in series (iso-stress, springs in series). The rules assume perfect bonding, aligned continuous fibres and a uniform distribution.

blocks.caption: Longitudinal modulus E_L (iso-strain) and transverse modulus E_T (iso-stress) of a unidirectional composite. Ef and Em are fibre and matrix moduli; Vf and Vm the volume fractions with Vf + Vm = 1.

blocks.markdown: **Why the longitudinal rule is a weighted average.** Under a stress along the fibres, fibre and matrix stretch by the same strain $\varepsilon$ (they are bonded). The stresses are $\sigma_f=E_f\varepsilon$ and $\sigma_m=E_m\varepsilon$, and the force is the sum of the fibre force and the matrix force: $\sigma_c=V_f\sigma_f+V_m\sigma_m=(V_fE_f+V_mE_m)\varepsilon$. For the transverse case the same stress acts on both phases, the strains add in proportion to the volume fractions, $\varepsilon_c=V_f\varepsilon_f+V_m\varepsilon_m$, and the inverse rule follows.

blocks.title: Moduli of a carbon/epoxy composite
blocks.prompt: A unidirectional composite has $V_f=0.60$ of carbon fibre ($E_f=230$ GPa) in epoxy ($E_m=3.5$ GPa). Calculate the longitudinal and transverse moduli.

steps.text: Longitudinal modulus from the iso-strain rule, with $V_m=0.40$.
Transverse modulus from the iso-stress rule: first the reciprocal.
Invert the reciprocal to obtain the modulus.
Compare: the longitudinal modulus is about 16 times larger, because the soft matrix controls the transverse response.

blocks.answer: E_L is about 139 GPa and E_T about 8.6 GPa.

blocks.caption: Carbon/epoxy (Ef = 230 GPa, Em = 3.5 GPa). E_L rises linearly with Vf, whereas E_T rises slowly until Vf is large.

blocks.markdown: **Share of the load.** In longitudinal loading the strain is equal, so the force carried by each phase is in proportion to $V E$. The fraction of the load carried by the fibres is therefore $F_f/F_c=V_fE_f/(V_fE_f+V_mE_m)$. Even a modest modulus ratio $E_f/E_m$ makes the fibres carry nearly all the load, which is why the matrix is mainly a binder.

blocks.caption: Fraction of the longitudinal load carried by the fibres, and the fibre stress in terms of the applied composite stress sigma_c (equal-strain assumption).

blocks.title: Load sharing in a composite bar
blocks.prompt: A bar of the carbon/epoxy composite above ($V_f=0.60$, $E_L=139.4$ GPa) has a cross-section of 200 mm$^2$ and carries a tensile force of 50 kN along the fibres. Find the fibre stress, the matrix stress and the fraction of the load carried by the fibres.

steps.text: Fibre and matrix stresses from the equal strain.
Fraction of the load carried by the fibres.

blocks.answer: Fibre stress about 412 MPa, matrix stress about 6.3 MPa; the fibres carry 99 % of the load.

blocks.markdown: **Why transverse properties are poor.** Perpendicular to the fibres the load must pass through the compliant matrix, so the modulus is governed by the matrix ($E_T$ is only about 1.5 to 3 times $E_m$ at $V_f\approx0.6$). Failure is worse than the modulus suggests. First, the soft matrix between closely spaced fibres is strained far more than the average strain, so a given applied strain produces a much larger local matrix strain (strain magnification). Second, the stress is concentrated around the fibres and at the fibre-matrix interface, which is weak. Third, voids and interface debonds act as cracks. The transverse tensile strength of a carbon/epoxy ply is typically only 40 to 60 MPa, against over 1500 MPa along the fibres.

blocks.title: Series and parallel bounds
blocks.text: The longitudinal rule (parallel, $E_L$) is an upper bound for the composite modulus in any direction, and the transverse rule (series, $E_T$) is a lower bound. For a unidirectional ply $E_T\ll E_L$, so loading across the fibres is a design weakness that laminates fix by orienting plies at several angles.

blocks.title: Assumptions behind the rules
blocks.text: The rules hold for aligned, continuous fibres with perfect bonding and no voids. They give excellent estimates for $E_L$, reasonable estimates of $E_T$ (which is slightly underpredicted, since the real fibre array constrains the matrix), and no direct information on strength, which is governed by defects and interface quality.

points: Longitudinal modulus follows the iso-strain average $E_L=V_fE_f+V_mE_m$; transverse modulus follows the iso-stress rule $1/E_T=V_f/E_f+V_m/E_m$ and is controlled by the matrix.
Under longitudinal loading the fibres carry the fraction $V_fE_f/E_L$ of the load, about 99 % for carbon/epoxy at $V_f=0.6$.
Transverse strength is low because the matrix strain is magnified between fibres, stress concentrates at the weak interface and voids act as cracks, so laminates use plies at several angles.

questions.stem: A unidirectional composite is loaded in tension parallel to its fibres. Which model and assumption give its modulus?

options.text: The iso-stress model: fibre and matrix carry equal stress and the strains add
The matrix alone governs the modulus, so $E_L=E_m$
The iso-strain model: fibre and matrix have equal strain and the stresses add in proportion to volume fraction
The fibre alone governs the modulus, so $E_L=E_f$

questions.correctOptionText: The iso-strain model: fibre and matrix have equal strain and the stresses add in proportion to volume fraction

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: iso-stress is the transverse model.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the matrix contributes only in proportion to $V_mE_m$ and the fibre usually dominates.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: bonded phases stretch together, so the parallel (iso-strain) rule applies.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the matrix still contributes its fraction, so it is $V_fE_f+V_mE_m$, which is less than $E_f$.

questions.explanation: Under tension along the fibres the two phases are bonded and extend by the same strain. The composite force is the sum of the two phase forces, which gives $E_L=V_fE_f+V_mE_m$.

questions.stem: A glass/polyester composite contains 45 % by volume of continuous aligned glass fibre ($E_f=72$ GPa) in a matrix of modulus $E_m=3.0$ GPa. Calculate the longitudinal modulus in GPa.
questions.explanation: By the rule of mixtures $E_L=V_fE_f+V_mE_m=0.45\times72+0.55\times3.0=32.4+1.65=34.05$ GPa. Almost all the stiffness comes from the glass fibres.

questions.stem: A composite has $V_f=0.40$ of continuous aligned fibres with $E_f=85$ GPa in a matrix with $E_m=3.2$ GPa. Calculate the transverse modulus in GPa.
questions.explanation: The iso-stress rule gives $1/E_T=0.40/85+0.60/3.2=0.004706+0.1875=0.192206$ GPa$^{-1}$. Inverting, $E_T=5.20$ GPa, less than twice the matrix modulus although the fibre is 27 times stiffer than the matrix.

questions.stem: A composite has $V_f=0.30$ of fibres with $E_f=72$ GPa in a matrix with $E_m=3.5$ GPa, loaded along the fibres. What fraction of the load do the fibres carry?

options.text: About 90 %
About 30 %
About 99 %
About 50 %

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is the volume fraction of the fibres; the load share is larger because they are stiffer.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this would need a much higher modulus ratio or fibre fraction.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: equal sharing would require equal moduli.

questions.explanation: The load share is $V_fE_f/(V_fE_f+V_mE_m)=21.6/(21.6+2.45)=0.898$. Although the fibres occupy 30 % of the volume, they carry about 90 % of the load because they are 20 times stiffer.

questions.stem: For a fixed fibre volume fraction, what happens to the fraction of the longitudinal load carried by the fibres as the ratio $E_f/E_m$ is increased?

options.text: It decreases towards zero
It stays equal to the volume fraction
It depends only on the matrix strength
It increases towards 100 %

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: a stiffer fibre takes more load, not less.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the share equals the volume fraction only when the moduli are equal.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: in the elastic range the share depends on moduli and not on strength.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: a stiffer fibre carries a larger share at the same strain.

questions.explanation: The share is $V_fE_f/(V_fE_f+V_mE_m)=1/(1+(V_m/V_f)(E_m/E_f))$. As $E_f/E_m$ grows, the matrix term shrinks and the share tends to 100 %.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the main reason why a unidirectional composite is much weaker perpendicular to the fibres?

options.text: The fibres are weaker in compression than in tension
Loads must pass through the weak matrix and fibre-matrix interface, where strain is magnified and stress concentrates
The matrix has a higher modulus than the fibres
The fibres break up when the load direction changes

questions.correctOptionText: Loads must pass through the weak matrix and fibre-matrix interface, where strain is magnified and stress concentrates

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: fibre compression behaviour does not govern transverse tensile failure.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the matrix strain between fibres is magnified and the interface and voids act as flaws.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the fibre is stiffer than the matrix in a composite, not the reverse.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the fibres are not damaged by the direction of the load; the matrix and interface fail.

questions.explanation: A transverse load passes in series through the matrix, so the local matrix strain is larger than the average strain. Combined with stress concentration at the interface and voids, this leads to failure at a small fraction of the longitudinal strength.

questions.stem: For a unidirectional composite with the same fibre fraction, how do the longitudinal modulus $E_L$ and the transverse modulus $E_T$ compare?

options.text: $E_T$ is greater, because the matrix surrounds the fibres
They are equal, since the same materials are used
They are equal only when the fibre fraction is 0.5
$E_L$ is greater, because the parallel rule gives the upper bound and the series rule the lower bound

questions.correctOptionText: $E_L$ is greater, because the parallel rule gives the upper bound and the series rule the lower bound

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the series estimate is always the lower value.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: composites are anisotropic, so the moduli differ whenever the phases differ.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: no fibre fraction between 0 and 1 gives equal values when $E_f\ne E_m$.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the iso-strain (parallel) estimate is the upper bound and the iso-stress (series) estimate is the lower bound.

questions.explanation: The arithmetic mean $V_fE_f+V_mE_m$ is always at least as large as the harmonic mean $[V_f/E_f+V_m/E_m]^{-1}$, with equality only if $E_f=E_m$. So $E_L\ge E_T$.

questions.stem: A bar of a unidirectional composite with $V_f=0.50$ of fibres ($E_f=200$ GPa) in a matrix ($E_m=4$ GPa) carries a tensile stress of 300 MPa averaged over the cross-section, applied along the fibres. Calculate the stress in the fibres, in MPa.
questions.explanation: The composite modulus is $E_L=0.5\times200+0.5\times4=102$ GPa, so the strain is $\varepsilon=300/102\,000=2.94\times10^{-3}$. The fibre stress is $E_f\varepsilon=200\,000\times2.94\times10^{-3}=588$ MPa, nearly twice the average stress.

questions.stem: Derive the rule of mixtures for the longitudinal modulus of a unidirectional composite and the expression for the fraction of the load carried by the fibres. Apply them to a composite with $V_f=0.5$, $E_f=70$ GPa and $E_m=3.5$ GPa.
markingGuide: States the assumption: bonded phases, equal strain $\varepsilon$ in fibre and matrix
questions.explanation: The equal-strain assumption turns the force balance into a weighted average of the moduli. With $V_fE_f=35$ GPa and $V_mE_m=1.75$ GPa, the fibres carry $35/36.75=95.2$ % of the load.

questions.stem: Explain why a unidirectional fibre composite is much weaker and less stiff transverse to the fibres than along them. Use the transverse rule of mixtures with $V_f=0.6$, $E_f=230$ GPa and $E_m=3.5$ GPa to quantify the stiffness, and give two reasons for the low transverse strength.
markingGuide: Transverse loading is iso-stress: the same stress passes through fibre and matrix in series, so strains add
$1/E_T=V_f/E_f+V_m/E_m=0.6/230+0.4/3.5=0.1169$ GPa$^{-1}$, giving $E_T\approx8.6$ GPa, only about 2.4 times $E_m$ and 6 % of $E_L$ (139.4 GPa)
Matrix strain is magnified between closely spaced fibres, so local strain is much greater than the average
Stress concentrates at the fibre-matrix interface, which is the weak link, and voids or debonds act as flaws
Design implication: use plies at several orientations or a laminate to supply transverse and shear properties
questions.explanation: A series arrangement is dominated by the more compliant phase, so the matrix controls the transverse response: $E_T=1/0.1169=8.55$ GPa. The strain magnification and interface weakness explain why strength falls even more than stiffness.
